title: Constituency Parsing
oneLiner: Group the words of a sentence into nested phrases, using grammar rules to find the possible structures and probabilities to pick the likeliest one.

what.html:
Constituency parsing builds a tree showing how words group into phrases: "the man" is a noun phrase, "saw the man" a verb phrase, and so on. A grammar lists which groupings are allowed; a chart stores pieces already built so nothing is repeated; and a probabilistic grammar scores each tree so the parser can choose.

Everyday version"I saw the man with the telescope": who has the telescope? You resolve it with common sense; a parser resolves it by asking which grouping its statistics make more probable.

why.html:
• Structure tells you who did what to whom.
  • Sentences can have hundreds of valid structures; parsers must find the plausible one fast.
  • The table-filling trick (CKY) is a model for many structured-prediction methods.

how.title: Ambiguity explodes
how.html: One "with the telescope" gives 2 trees; add "on the hill" and "in Texas" and you get 14; five such phrases give 132.

how.title: A rulebook of phrases
how.html: Rules like "sentence = noun phrase + verb phrase" build trees. Each phrase is named after its key word: a noun phrase around a noun, a verb phrase around a verb.

how.title: Architect or builder
how.html: Start from "sentence" and break it down (top-down), or start from the words and combine them (bottom-up). Either way, naive parsers redo the same work after every wrong guess.

how.title: Remember what you built
how.html: A chart parser writes every finished phrase into a table, and a dot inside each rule marks how far it has got: "noun phrase = article • adjective noun" means the article has been found.

how.title: Add probabilities
how.html: Every rule gets a probability; a tree's score is the product. For "astronomers saw stars with ears", attaching "with ears" to "stars" scores 0.00091, beating 0.00068 for "saw … with ears".

how.title: Fill the triangle
how.html: Rewrite the grammar so each rule has two parts (or one word). Then fill a triangular table: best scores for every one-word span, then two-word spans, and so on, up to the whole sentence.

how.title: What probabilities miss
how.html: Plain rule probabilities ignore the actual words ("give him a book" vs "sleep him a book") and where in the tree a phrase sits.

how.title: Grading a parser
how.html: Compare its labelled phrases with a human-made tree: precision (how many of its phrases are right), recall (how many true phrases it found), and their balance, F1.

demo.html: Before CKY can run, every rule must have exactly two parts or one word. Pick the fix each rule needs.

example.html:
Over-guessing. A parser that proposes 100 phrases for a short sentence might include all 6 correct ones (recall 100%), but only 6% of its guesses are right (precision 6%), so its F1 is about 0.11.

Supplementary Swap "best" for "sum" when filling the CKY table and you get the total probability of the sentence, which lets a grammar be trained even without hand-drawn trees.

misunderstandings: Ambiguous sentences have many valid trees.
The most probable tree is the true meaning.
It's what the statistics favour, without world knowledge.
High recall means a good parser.
takeaways: Attachment ambiguity grows as the Catalan numbers (2, 5, 14, …, 132).
CFG = (N, Σ, R, S); phrases have heads.
Charts store partial results (dotted rules, agenda).
PCFG: P(T) = Π P(rule); CKY finds the best tree in O(n³).
PCFGs lack lexical and structural context; evaluate with labelled P/R/F1.
thirty: Structural ambiguity (I saw the man with the telescope) multiplies parses as Catalan numbers (2, 5, 14, 132). A CFG (N, Σ, R, S) builds phrases with heads (NP, VP, PP). Top-down parsing expands from S (may mismatch words); bottom-up combines words (may build useless pieces); naive backtracking repeats work. Chart parsers store constituents and use dotted rules, an agenda and active arcs. PCFGs give rule probabilities summing to 1 per left-hand side; P(T) = Π P(r): astronomers saw stars with ears, T1 = 0.0006804 (VP attach) vs T2 = 0.0009072 (NP attach). CKY needs CNF (A → B C, A → a) and fills π[i, j, A] by span (NP = 0.3 × 0.4 × 0.02 = 0.0024) in O(n³). PCFGs ignore words (give vs sleep) and structural context (subject pronouns). PARSEVAL uses labelled precision, recall and F1 (100 guesses, 6 gold: P = 0.06, R = 1).
